title: Checkpoint: Skyscrapers
objective: After this level you can explain what makes skyscrapers possible and how they stay up.
summary: 'Skyscraper' was a sail before it was a building (1888, Chicago). New York's 1916 zoning, after the Equitable's shadow, shaped wedding-cake towers. Frames, elevators and wind strategies do the rest.

cards.headline: Skyscrapers recap: before it was a building, a skyscraper was a sail.
cards.body: In 1794, a skyscraper was a light sail at the very top of a ship's mast. Here's how the word climbed onto buildings, and how one city's law gave its skyline a shape.

cards.headline: A word for tall things
cards.body: The word was used for all sorts of high-reaching things, even a racehorse, before it was first recorded for a very tall city building in 1888, in a Chicago context. That's the Chicago of Level 61's Chicago school. Other languages chose the same picture: German says Wolkenkratzer, "cloud scraper," and French says gratte-ciel, "scrape-sky."

cards.headline: The law that stepped the skyline
cards.body: In 1915, New York's Equitable Building rose straight up, with no setbacks, to 538 feet, and cast a seven-acre shadow over its neighbors. The city answered with its 1916 Zoning Resolution, the nation's first comprehensive zoning ordinance, which controlled the size and shape of buildings. It fostered slender towers and tiered "wedding cake" buildings. Those steps began with a shadow, not with the wind.

mascot.line: Next time you see a stepped New York tower, you're looking at a law, drawn in stone.
